subject: Creativity
title: Oblique Strategies: Brian Eno's Creative Cards
description: A short lesson to help you apply Oblique Strategies: Brian Eno's Creative Cards.

hook.text: Stuck in the studio, Brian Eno would draw a card: 'Use an unacceptable color.' 'Honor thy error as a hidden intention.'

buildup.text: Eno and Peter Schmidt created Oblique Strategies in 1975 — a deck of cards with cryptic creative prompts.

discovery.text: Each card imposes an unexpected constraint or perspective shift that breaks creative blocks through lateral disruption.

twist.text: David Bowie used them for his Berlin trilogy. Coldplay used them for Viva la Vida.

climax.text: They work because they externalize decision-making. When you're stuck, the card decides — removing the paralysis of.

punchline.text: When you're paralyzed by options, let a random card decide.

details.summary: Oblique Strategies is a deck of cards created by Brian Eno and Peter Schmidt, each containing a cryptic instruction like Use an old idea or Honor thy error as a hidden intention. Drawing a random card when stuck provides an unexpected creative prompt.
details.whyItMatters: Oblique Strategies demonstrates that creative blocks can be broken through randomness and ambiguity. The cards have been used to produce landmark albums and are a model for breaking habitual creative patterns.
takeaways: Each card contains a brief, ambiguous instruction
The randomness forces the creator to think from a new angle
Eno used the cards to produce some of the most influential albums in music

faq.question: How do Oblique Strategies work?
faq.answer: When stuck in a creative process, draw a random card and apply its instruction to your current situation. The instruction is deliberately ambiguous so you must interpret it, and that interpretation forces a new perspective on the work.

faq.question: Are Oblique Strategies only for musicians?
faq.answer: No. Although Eno created them for music production, the cards work for any creative discipline. Writers, designers, programmers, and business strategists have all used them successfully because the prompts address creative thinking, not specific mediums.
